title: The fast of Dawud
hookLine: a day on, a day off, the most beloved fast (Bukhari)
carry: a day on, a day off

cards: What do you do with someone who wants to do too much good? Abdullah ibn Amr was a companion with a big plan.

Word reached the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that Abdullah had vowed to fast every single day and stand in prayer every single night, for as long as he lived. The Prophet came to him and asked if it was true. It was.
What came next wasn't praise, and it wasn't a scolding either. It was a negotiation, step by step, that ended at a fast with a name.

teach.b: First, the bargaining, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet tells Abdullah: you can't keep that up. Fast and break your fast, sleep and stand in prayer.
Fast three days a month. Abdullah says he can do more. More is offered, and he asks for more again, until the Prophet says: then fast the fast of Dawud.
Fast a day, and break a day. When Abdullah asks for still more, the answer is that there is nothing better than that. Second, the reason.

teach.h: YOUR BODY HAS A RIGHT OVER YOU.
teach.b: In the same report the Prophet tells him his body has a right over him, and his eyes, and his wife, and his guests. Worship isn't meant to swallow the rest of a life. Third, the name.
Dawud is David, the prophet the Qur'an remembers for the psalms he was given.
Another hadith in Bukhari says the most beloved fast to Allah is the fast of Dawud, who fasted one day and not the next, and the most beloved prayer is his: sleeping, rising, and sleeping again.
A rhythm, not a marathon. Fourth, the ending. Abdullah lives long, and in old age he wishes he had taken the Prophet's easier offer.

teach.h: AN OLD MAN KEEPS HIS WORD.
teach.b: Another version in Bukhari says he kept to his word anyway: a companion, preserved in the collection, admitting he asked for too much.
The same thread runs through this week: the fast bends, missed days are made up, some feed instead, the fast is a shield, two days a week, three days a month.
And today, at the far edge of what's encouraged, a day on and a day off, with rest built in.

how: Some Muslims keep the fast of Dawud, fasting every other day, and the story of Abdullah ibn Amr is told as a caution against taking on more than one can sustain.

games.q: what does “the fast of dawud” mean?
o: fasting every single day of life, kept as a vow
a night-long vigil of prayer, kept once a week
fasting every other day, named for the prophet David

games.q: the fast of Dawud — tap the pairs.
p: fasted a day, broke a day
Abdullah wished he'd taken the easier offer

s: the Prophet praised Abdullah's plan to fast every day
he talked him down: fast and break your fast, sleep and stand in prayer.
the fast of Dawud means one day fasting, one day eating
a day on, a day off, and nothing better than that, the report says.
Dawud's prayer meant staying awake the whole night
the hadith describes sleeping, rising to pray, and sleeping again.

games.q: you're the Prophet. a young man tells you he'll fast every day and pray every night for life. what do you say?
o: you can't keep that up; fast and break your fast, sleep and pray.
games.why: he talks him down, step by step, to a day on and a day off, and reminds him that his body has a right over him.

practice: Breathe in and out slowly, and notice the rhythm: effort, then rest; neither is better than the other, and the breath needs both.
Then think of one thing you've been doing every single day without a break, and ask what a day off from it would look like. Don't decide anything; just let the question breathe with you.

wordCard.voice: The fast of Dawud. Fasting one day and eating the next, named for the prophet David, and called in Bukhari the most beloved fast to Allah. Today's word.

orig.note: sawm is fasting; Dawud is the prophet David.

carryVoice: Your line: a day on, a day off. Rest is part of the rhythm. Another week, done.
